newsitem.title: USA: U.S. increasingly open on problems with Russia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. increasingly open on problems with Russia.

text.p: With President Boris Yeltsin set to undergo risky heart surgery and the U.S. election almost over, the Clinton administration is talking more openly about its concerns over anti-Western trends in Moscow.

Although its bottom line remains essentially optimistic, senior American officials acknowledge serious problems with Yeltsin's government -- not Yeltsin himself -- and have begun to warn of consequences if these tendencies continue.

The most authoritative expression of these concerns came last week in a speech by Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, the top U.S. policymaker on Russia who is considered likely to be the next National Security Adviser if President Bill Clinton is re-elected on Tuesday as most predict.
The address was made to a stellar audience at the Harriman Institute of Columbia University in New York City but many Russia experts in Washington were only vaguely aware of it.

In it, Talbott said Russia and the United States still harbour Cold War fears about each other five years after the fall of communism and he warned that this festering suspicion could undermine future cooperation. He specifically attacked unamed members of Russia's "foreign policy elite" for holding worst-case Cold War stereotypes about the United States.
"Many of them have made clear that they believe America's real strategy, indeed this administration's real strategy, is actually to weaken Russia, even divide it," Talbott said.

He denied this was the case and warned that "if Russians overindulge their misplaced suspicions that we want to keep them down ... the result could be that we will indeed cooperate less and compete more."

It also would be a mistake for Russians to repeat an error they made during most of this century -- "defining their security at the expense of everyone else's and misdefining security itself as the expensive and wasteful capacity to destroy and intimidate," Talbott said.

As they move into the 21st century, Russia and the United States had major choices to make and a key test was how they managed NATO's plans to expand into eastern Europe by 1999, a U.S.-led effort Russians do not view benignly, he said.

The admonition comes at a critical time for Russia, where an intensive Kremlin power struggle is under way as Yeltsin undergoes major heart surgery, possibly as early as Tuesday. If Yeltsin dies or is incapacitated there could be a sustained period of instability, experts say.

Meanwhile, the top U.S. military officer, Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, will visit Moscow on Tuesday for talks with his new Russian counterpart, Chief of the General Staff Gen. Viktor Nikolayevich Samsonov, the Defence Department said on Monday. There was no indication the visit was connected to Yeltsin's impending operation.
Talbott's warning also came as Washington and its NATO allies were set to begin making concrete decisions on enlarging the Western alliance.

U.S. diplomacy toward Russia has been pretty much static during the U.S. election campaign, but that will end on Tuesday and whoever emerges as president is expected to launch new initiatives on that front.

Russia and the United States have been moving for some time away from their cooperation heyday after the fall of communism. But it is recent experiences that prompted Talbott to make an issue of what one official called a tendency in Moscow toward "bad habits."
"This is Yeltsin's government we're having trouble with and there have been a lot of different examples of that in the last month or so," the official told Reuters.

Among other things, Russia reneged on a regional missile defences accord and efforts to get Russia to sign a special charter with NATO has produced more anti-expansion rhetoric than concrete cooperation from Moscow.
Also, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry was rebuffed by parliamentary hardliners when he made an appeal for approval of the START 2 nuclear arms treaty in Moscow last month.

U.S. officials do not fault Yeltsin, whom they consider a democrat. They say he and Clinton have close personal and working ties, but other Kremlin officials have exploited Yeltsin's illness and health-related absences to thwart policies on which the two presidents have agreed.

Russian expert Clifford Gaddy of the Brookings Institution said Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais was one official who had shifted both in rhetoric and behaviour from the solidily pro-democratic, pro-reform views he earlier spoused.
Beyond that, Russian economic reforms are stymied while Russian economists more openly espouse "retrograde" policies and talk about being victimised by Western policies, he said.
